Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) -- Demonstrators stormed a hotel Saturday where Asian leaders were to meet, forcing the indefinite postponement of the Association of South East Asian Nations summit. Thousands of anti-government protesters block a busy intersection during rush hour in Bangkok. Participating Asian leaders were on their way out of the country, according to Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva. He declared a state of emergency in Chonburi province and the southern coastal city of Pattaya, where the summit was to be held, but rescinded the order hours afterward. Thousands of "red shirt" protesters, named for the color of their attire, have rallied for days to demand Abhisit's resignation. The demonstrators flooded into the summit site after smashing through the hotel's glass doors, but were otherwise nonviolent. Hundreds of them streamed in, without police interference. Protesters hugged the officers and shook their hands. The red shirts have given the prime minister repeated deadlines to resign, but those have come and gone. United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon he was disappointed by the summit's delay. "I understand the circumstances that led the Thai government to take this difficult decision. While I had hoped to have exchanges with the leaders of ASEAN and its dialogue partners, I continue to look forward to engaging again with them in the near future," Ban said. "I strongly value the long-standing relationship between ASEAN and the United Nations, and their cooperation in various fields. I hope for an early restoration of normalcy in Thailand and for the settlement of differences through dialogue and peaceful means," he added. The protesters are loyal to former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was ousted in a 2006 coup. Thaksin now lives outside of Thailand. The protesters have said Abhisit's government was not democratically elected and want him to resign and schedule elections. Abhisit, who has held the position for four months, has rejected calls for him to step down. Lawmakers named the 44-year-old, Oxford University-educated Abhisit prime minister in December in the wake of months of demonstrations against Thaksin and his ruling party, People Power Party. On Tuesday, protesters rushed Abhisit's motorcade while it was struck in traffic. He escaped unharmed. Protesters opposed to Thaksin took to the streets last year wearing yellow shirts, occupied the Government House and blockaded Bangkok's major international airport, stranding throngs of tourists who provide much of the country's revenue. The demonstrations ended in early December when a court ruled that the People Power Party was guilty of electoral fraud and threw Thaksin's brother-in-law out of the prime minister's seat. The red shirt protesters said this week they would not take over the airports. Dan Rivers and Kocha Olarn contributed to this report.

The demonstrators view the current government as illegitimate and have demanded that Abhisit dissolve parliament and call new elections.

The storming of the summit represents a dramatic escalation in Thailand's prolonged political turmoil, which has seen competing factions repeatedly take to the streets in recent years.

The failure to hold the summit deals a significant blow to Thailand's international standing and raises fresh questions about political stability in a nation that has long been regarded as a regional economic hub and popular tourist destination.

Analysts said the images of a collapsed international summit could have lasting effects on investor confidence and Thailand's reputation as a reliable host for diplomatic gatherings.

As night fell, the situation in Pattaya remained tense, with security forces working to restore order and clear demonstrators from the summit area.

# ASEAN Summit Collapses as Protesters Storm Venue; Thailand Declares State of Emergency

**PATTAYA, Thailand** — A major summit of Southeast Asian leaders collapsed in chaos after anti-government protesters breached security and stormed the conference venue, forcing the emergency evacuation of foreign heads of state and dealing a severe blow to Thailand's international standing.

## Summit Disrupted

Hundreds of demonstrators, many wearing the red shirts that identify them as supporters of the anti-government movement, pushed through police lines and shattered glass doors to enter the luxury beachfront hotel hosting the East Asia Summit. The intrusion forced organizers to abruptly cancel the gathering, which had brought together leaders from across Asia.

Several foreign leaders were evacuated by helicopter from the hotel rooftop, while others were rushed to safety amid concerns for their security. The dramatic scenes of world leaders fleeing a summit venue broadcast images of instability to a global audience, embarrassing the host government at a moment it had hoped to project competence and control.

## State of Emergency

In response to the security breach, the Thai government declared a state of emergency in Pattaya and surrounding areas. The prime minister, appearing on national television, condemned the protesters and vowed that those responsible would face legal consequences for jeopardizing national security and Thailand's reputation abroad.

The emergency declaration granted authorities expanded powers to restore order, including the ability to impose restrictions on public gatherings and deploy additional security forces. Officials scrambled to reassure the international community that the safety of visiting dignitaries remained a top priority even as the summit itself was abandoned.

## Background: A Nation Divided

The disruption reflected the deep and enduring political fault lines that have fractured Thai society. At the heart of the conflict lies a struggle between rival political movements often characterized by their signature colors.

The "red shirt" movement broadly represents supporters of the ousted former prime minister and draws significant backing from rural and working-class Thais, particularly in the north and northeast. Their opponents, associated with the "yellow shirt" movement, have generally drawn support from the urban middle class, royalist establishment, and elements of the military and bureaucracy.

The divide traces back to political upheaval that saw a popularly elected but controversial leader removed from power, followed by cycles of protest, legal challenges, and shifting governments. Each side has accused the other of undermining democracy and the rule of law, with the red shirts arguing that their electoral victories have been repeatedly overturned by unelected institutions, while their opponents allege corruption and abuses of power.

## Broader Implications

The collapse of the summit carried significant regional consequences. As host, Thailand had sought to demonstrate leadership within Southeast Asia's principal diplomatic bloc. Instead, the failure to guarantee even the basic security of an international meeting raised questions about the government's grip on power and the stability of one of the region's key economies.

Analysts warned that the confrontation marked a dangerous escalation, with the potential for further violence as neither side showed signs of backing down. The events underscored how domestic political turmoil can spill over into the international arena, with lasting damage to a nation's credibility and diplomatic ambitions.

As security forces moved to reestablish control, the fundamental grievances driving the unrest remained unresolved, leaving open the prospect of continued instability in the days and weeks ahead.

# Thailand's Political Turmoil: The 2009 Crisis

## Background and Context

Thailand's political landscape in 2009 was shaped by years of division stemming from the 2006 military coup that ousted Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. A telecommunications billionaire turned populist politician, Thaksin had won landslide electoral victories in 2001 and 2005, building a devoted following particularly among rural voters in the north and northeast through policies including affordable healthcare and village development funds.

His removal from power while attending a UN meeting in New York set the stage for years of instability. Thaksin subsequently went into self-imposed exile abroad, though his political influence remained potent.

## The Rise of the Red Shirts

The United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship (UDD), whose supporters became known as the "Red Shirts," emerged as a powerful pro-Thaksin movement. Drawing heavily from rural constituencies and working-class urban populations, they positioned themselves as champions of democracy against what they characterized as an entrenched establishment of military leaders, royalists, and Bangkok elites.

The Red Shirts stood in opposition to the "Yellow Shirts" of the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD), who had helped precipitate Thaksin's downfall and generally aligned with royalist and establishment interests.

## Abhisit's Ascension

Abhisit Vejjajiva, the Oxford-educated leader of the Democrat Party, became Prime Minister in December 2008. His path to power came not through a general election but through a parliamentary vote after the pro-Thaksin People's Power Party was dissolved by court order and coalition partners shifted their allegiance.

Critics, particularly Red Shirt supporters, viewed Abhisit's government as illegitimate—installed through judicial and political maneuvering rather than the popular mandate. This perception fueled much of the subsequent unrest.

## The 2009 Confrontations

Tensions escalated dramatically in April 2009. Red Shirt demonstrators mobilized in large numbers, and the crisis reached a dramatic peak when protesters disrupted the ASEAN Summit in Pattaya. The chaos forced the evacuation of visiting Asian leaders—some by helicopter—and led to the summit's cancellation, an internationally embarrassing episode for the Thai government.

The unrest spread to Bangkok, where confrontations between demonstrators and security forces turned violent. The government declared a state of emergency, and troops were deployed to disperse crowds. The clashes, which came to be known by some as part of the "Songkran riots" (coinciding with the Thai New Year period), resulted in deaths and numerous injuries.

Thaksin himself remained a central figure throughout, addressing his supporters via video link from abroad and calling for continued resistance against the Abhisit government.

## The Aftermath

The 2009 turmoil ultimately subsided, with the government reasserting control. However, the underlying grievances remained unresolved. The events of that year proved to be a precursor to even larger and deadlier confrontations in 2010, when Red Shirt protests occupied central Bangkok for weeks before a military crackdown resulted in significant loss of life.

## Analysis

The 2009 crisis exposed deep fault lines in Thai society—divisions along class, regional, and ideological lines that transcended simple partisan politics. The conflict reflected fundamental disagreements about the nature of Thai democracy, the role of traditional institutions, and questions of representation and legitimacy that would continue to define the nation's politics for years to come.

---

*Note: This account synthesizes the general historical narrative of these events. For academic or professional purposes, readers should consult primary sources and contemporaneous reporting for specific details, casualty figures, and direct quotations.*
